steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Every evening, when the sky’s last marigold band bled into ink, Elias Vane climbed the spiral staircase of Gullhook Lighthouse. The lantern room, a glass crown on a basalt pillar, was his kingdom; the sea, his only subject.  

For forty years he had kept the light. Storms shattered ships and wars reshaped maps, but Elias remained, winding the clockwork, polishing lenses until they shone like captive moons. The keeper before him once said a lighthouse exists for sailors who never learn your name. Elias grew old believing that was enough—until one wind-scoured December night.

That evening, the barometer fell hard. The horizon vanished behind slate walls of rain. Far below, the tide smashed itself into fireworks of foam. Elias trimmed the wick, glad to have something steady to touch. He listened for the foghorn’s distant croak and heard instead a trembling voice from the radio, half-drowned in static:

“—Mayday. Engines gone. Drifting toward the Teeth.”

The Teeth were a row of black, razor rocks three miles offshore. Elias pictured them instinctively: they had claimed hulls thicker than a man’s faith. He thumbed the transmitter. “Mayday received. You keep your eyes on the light.”  

But the light itself was faltering; the storm’s breath seeped through a cracked pane, licking at the flame. He fetched a spare mantle, yet when he returned, the lantern’s heart sputtered, then died. Darkness swallowed the tower. Below, the radio crackled one last time, then fell silent.

Elias, seventy-three years old and arthritic, stared into the black as if it were judgment. He could swear he felt every lost sailor he’d ever failed pressing against the night. Then he surprised himself: he began to run. Down the stairwell, boots slamming stone, past the storeroom, out into the gale where rain felt like gravel.

He reached the generator shed, yanked the cord—it coughed, resisted, then roared awake. Lights winked along the tower’s spine. Back upstairs, he relit the lamp. Fresh kerosene hissed, glass warmed, and the Fresnel lens caught the newborn flame, multiplying it a hundredfold. The beacon burst across the sea: one flash every five seconds, its pulse sturdier than Elias’s own.

An hour crawled by. Lightning revealed nothing but heaving water, yet Elias wouldn’t leave his post. Finally, a small white flare arched in the distance. Search-and-rescue’s reply rose red, circling like a guardian star. Only then did Elias sink onto a wooden stool, chest aching with relief.

At dawn, the storm had limped east. A single tug escorted a battered fishing boat into harbor. From deck to tower, a figure waved—a silhouette against the sun, indistinct but unmistakably alive. Elias lifted a trembling hand in return.  

He understood, perhaps for the first time, that the lighthouse was not merely a warning. It was a promise: Someone is awake. Someone is waiting. And while he could still coax light from darkness, that promise was his to keep.
